:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We know how to integrate $\cos{x}.$ But how do we integrate $\cos{3x}?$ 

To compute

$$
\int \cos{3x} \, \textrm dx,
$$

we can use substitution. If we let $u=3x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u.
$$

Finally, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** After solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+C) & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\cdot 3 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=\dfrac x 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac 1 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =3\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x & =2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot 3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡u+C \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=6x+\dfrac \pi 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =\dfrac 1 6\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int 2x \cos{(x^2)}\,\textrm d x.$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then we have

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} \cos({\overbrace{x^2}^u})\,\textrm d x.
$$

In other words, the factor multiplying the trigonometric function is the derivative of the argument! Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

So, let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$
